stem: A 24-year-old adult previously received BCG vaccination. A clinician chooses an interferon-gamma release assay when evaluating TB infection because of a possible vaccination-related effect on another available test. Which of the following comparisons best explains that choice?

options.label: A
options.text: Prior vaccination makes chest imaging measure the same immune response
options.explanation: Chest radiography evaluates disease rather than the antigen-stimulated white-cell response measured by IGRA. Prior BCG does not make these tests interchangeable measurements here.
options.misconception: Treats chest imaging and an antigen-stimulated white-cell response as interchangeable measurements.

options.label: B
options.text: Prior vaccination can affect skin testing but not the blood assay
options.explanation: BCG can produce a false-positive tuberculin skin test but does not cause a false-positive IGRA. This difference explains the choice when vaccination-related confounding is the concern.
options.misconception: No misconception: BCG-related false-positive effects differ between the skin test and IGRA.

options.label: C
options.text: Prior vaccination can affect the blood assay but not skin testing
options.explanation: This reverses the stated comparison. The recognized BCG-related false-positive effect concerns the skin test, not the interferon-gamma release assay selected for this evaluation.
options.misconception: Reverses which infection assay is subject to the specified BCG-related false-positive effect.

options.label: D
options.text: Prior vaccination causes equal false-positive effects in both assays
options.explanation: The tests differ in their susceptibility to the specified BCG-related effect. Treating them as equally confounded removes the reason for choosing the blood assay here.
options.misconception: Assumes BCG confounds both assays equally and overlooks the reason for selecting IGRA.

options.label: E
options.text: Prior vaccination makes either result sufficient to diagnose active disease
options.explanation: Neither infection-test result alone establishes active TB. Selecting an assay less affected by BCG does not eliminate the need for a separate disease evaluation.
options.misconception: Confuses reduced vaccination-related confounding with proof of active TB from either infection test.

context: Learning objective: distinguish the effect of prior BCG on TB testing methods. BCG can cause a false-positive skin test, whereas the supplied IGRA interpretation is not confounded in that way.
